body:
> For example, [this tutorial](https://blogs.oracle.com/enterprisetechtips/true-abstraction:-composite-ui-components-in-jsf-20-part-1) about Java Server Faces includes elements in the JSF namespace in what seems to be intended as a conforming XHTML page.

This link doesn't work for me, but JSF is not transmitted to the browser. It is parsed by the web server and (x)html is generated from it.

If you use the XHTML syntax, you can indeed put "foreign"-namespaced elements into your HTML document. It's also always going to be non-conforming, because arbitrary foreign-namespaced elements don't have widely-understood semantics - search engines, accessibility tools, etc have no idea how to handle such elements.

(Note that nothing of the XHTML syntax should be construed as being done for any particular advantage. The syntax is specified because it exists in the wild in sufficient quantity to be worth documenting, not because it's a good idea.)

> This link doesn't work for me, but JSF is not transmitted to the browser. It is parsed by the web server and (x)html is generated from it.

Thanks (the link must have ceased to work recently), I have changed it for an example page. I know that the JSF markup is not transmitted to the client, but still, I always thought that one of the good points of this technology is that the server-side pages are supposed to be valid XTHML pages, which permits to check their validty with standard tooling. This is only true if indeed foreign elements can be included. Hence, my question.

> If you use the XHTML syntax, you can indeed put "foreign"-namespaced elements into your HTML document.

In what sense do you mean that I can? If you mean, in the sense of the specs, isn’t it the same thing as saying that it would be conforming? I may have missed something here.

> It's also always going to be non-conforming, because arbitrary foreign-namespaced elements don't have widely-understood semantics - search engines, accessibility tools, etc have no idea how to handle such elements.

If I understand correctly, Chapter 14, The XML syntax, seems to cover what browsers should do with such foreign elements. Indeed this does not give them proper semantics, of course. This is not a decisive reason to make it non-compliant. I still would find this handy, to allow for extensions (some browsers would understand some of these foreign elements, which would allow for richer interpretation). RDF for HTML seems like a good example. (Of course, the question whether it would be a good idea that it be non-compliant is different than the question: is it indeed non-compliant, and should this be clarified in the specs.)
 
> (Note that nothing of the XHTML syntax should be construed as being done for any particular advantage. The syntax is specified because it exists in the wild in sufficient quantity to be worth documenting, not because it's a good idea.)

If you have a few good references to back up this claim, I’d be interested. I currently view a few advantages to XHTML (such as its strict syntax and the fact that it is XML, a good language with good tooling, IMHO), but I am very sure that this issue is not the proper place to debate this.

> In what sense do you mean that I can? If you mean, in the sense of the specs, isn’t it the same thing as saying that it would be conforming? I may have missed something here.

I just meant that it is possible to do so; you can write the syntax into your document and get the expected DOM.

> If I understand correctly, Chapter 14, The XML syntax, seems to cover what browsers should do with such foreign elements. Indeed this does not give them proper semantics, of course.

Right, they have a mechanical definition, just zero semantics. However, people often *think* that elements in random namespaces have semantics. (And they do, in whatever context they're understood in. Just not in the important context here, which is a standard web browser and associated tooling presenting a page to a user.)

> If you have a few good references to back up this claim, I’d be interested. I currently view a few advantages to XHTML (such as its strict syntax and the fact that it is XML, a good language with good tooling, IMHO), but I am very sure that this issue is not the proper place to debate this.

Yeah, it's not. ^_^ I'd have to hunt down blog posts discussing this, which I don't have the time to do, but the short of it is that XML's strict parsing is dramatically incompatible-in-practice with the public web. Most "XHTML" currently on the web does not have the right invocations to be parsed as XML, and is instead parsed as HTML; this is a good thing, because most of it is *incorrect* XML anyway and would fail to display. Humans, in the large, don't seem to be able to write webpages as valid XML. There are various reasons, but the fact that quite a lot of webpages are produced from string concatenation (rather than from a proper DOM-building toolchain) is probably a major contributing factor.

This is separate from any discussion about XML as a language for other purposes, which it may be well-suited for.
